infrastructure: Iceland's abundant geothermal and hydroelectric energy (virtually 100% renewable) makes it one of the world's most attractive locations for energy-intensive AI data centres.
Strong fibre broadband connectivity and full 5G coverage across populated areas.
Several hyperscale data centres operate in Iceland, drawn by cheap green electricity and natural cooling.
talent: University of Iceland has an AI research group; Reykjavik University's School of Computer Science is internationally active.
Small population (370,000) fundamentally limits the absolute talent pool.
High education levels and English proficiency make Icelanders effective AI adopters.
governance: Iceland consistently ranks among the world's top nations for democracy, press freedom, and rule of law.
The Data Protection Authority (Persónuvernd) is an active, GDPR-aligned regulator.
As an EEA member, Iceland adopts EU AI Act provisions, providing regulatory alignment without full EU membership.
investment: Data centre investment is significant relative to Iceland's size, with major operators expanding capacity.
Limited domestic VC for AI startups; investment mainly flows into infrastructure.
Government R&D support through Rannís supports innovation, though at small scale.
economic_readiness: A small, highly developed economy with advanced fisheries, tourism, and financial sectors beginning AI adoption.
High per-capita income supports enterprise AI spending, despite limited market scale.
Energy sector AI optimisation (geothermal management) is a notable domestic AI application.
